okr.objective: Coventina is a British water goddess known from sculptures at a Northumberland well.
key_results: Sculptures at a sacred well in Northumberland show Coventina pouring water from an urn.
She chiefly ruled the Carrawburgh River and was also honored in Spain and France with the titles Augusta and Sancta.
Like other Celtic water goddesses, she may have had a healing aspect.
Her well shrine stands at Carrawburgh beside Hadrian's Wall.
Surviving reliefs portray her as a water-nymph.
Excavations in 1876 recovered a cache of about 14,000 ancient coins from the well.

text: Coventina is a goddess of wells and streams whom Romano-British worshippers honored during the Roman occupation of Britain. A shrine with a well stood at Carrawburgh in south Northumberland, beside Hadrian's Wall. Carved reliefs from the site show her as a water-nymph. One relief depicts her reclining and tipping water from an urn. Another shows her among water plants, pouring her vessel over them. Inscriptions style her Augusta and Sancta, high and holy. Devotees carried her cult to Spain and Gaul. Excavations in 1876 recovered about 14,000 ancient coins from her well. The hoard shows how many worshippers cast offerings into the water.
